note: Chaining patterns — the reusable escalation moves practitioners actually use, each grounded in a named researcher's primary write-up or book (not a tutorial). pihunt-gadgets patterns cross-links these to the live gadget-graph chains: for a chain granting capability X, it names the pattern X instantiates, the NEXT link that pattern predicts, and the source so the reasoning is auditable. Match order: explicit maps_to first, then grant_match substring against the chain's grants[]. Keep sources to work the author is known for; add a pattern when a new chain has no match rather than forcing a bad fit.

name: Object-ID BOLA → sibling-verb sweep → cross-tenant read/write
tells: a per-object id (UUID/slug) in the path
ownership proven on GET but the write/state verbs on the SAME object untested
a resource resolved from a global store after only a parent-scope check
predicts: Never stop at the verb that leaked. Enumerate EVERY sibling verb on the same object id — read, write-credential (upload/part-urls), state-change (cancel/fork/pause/resume/rollback) — the ownership check is forgotten on the less-obvious verbs, not the GET. Then push a cross-tenant READ toward takeover by pivoting whatever it leaks (presigned URL, secret, internal id).

sources.who: Sam Curry, Brett Buerhaus et al.
sources.work: Web Hackers vs. The Auto Industry (BOLA across sibling endpoints → full vehicle/account takeover)
The Web Application Hacker's Handbook, 2nd ed. — test access control on every object reference, per role
Real-World Bug Hunting (No Starch) — IDOR field reports

name: BOLA/BFLA on a key-management endpoint → stored-credential disclosure
tells: an endpoint that stores/lists/regenerates provider keys or tokens keyed by an object uuid
list/regenerate siblings next to a create
the key is BYOK / third-party (blast radius leaves the platform)
predicts: Treat the key store as an object store: test cross-account LIST and per-uuid GET first (disclosure), then REGENERATE (silent takeover of the victim's provider spend/data). A read here is not the end — the leaked provider key is itself a pivot into the victim's upstream (OpenAI/Anthropic) account.

sources.work: Web Hackers vs. The Auto Industry — admin/API-key endpoints chained to mass account access
Real-World Bug Hunting — chaining IDOR into credential/secret exposure

name: SSRF via URL-parser confusion + allowlist/redirect bypass
tells: a server-side fetcher that takes a user URL (data-source ingest, image_url, webhook, doc fetch)
a host allowlist enforced on the INITIAL url before resolution
a fetcher that follows cross-origin 30x
predicts: The validator and the requester disagree about the host — exploit the gap: userinfo/@ tricks (http://ok.host@evil/), an allowlisted host that off-origin-redirects, IDNA/parser diffs. Confirm reach to an internal target ONLY through the approved sheriff, with a nonce + a distinct-nonce negative control, then chain SSRF→metadata/credential→RCE as the parser-confusion GitHub Enterprise demo did.

sources.work: A New Era of SSRF — Exploiting URL Parser in Trending Programming Languages (Black Hat USA / DEF CON 25); SSRF→RCE via a 4-bug chain

name: Web cache deception / poisoning → serve an authed response to the attacker → ATO
tells: a CDN/edge cache in front of authenticated pages
a cache key that ignores a header or a path suffix (unkeyed input)
a URL shape that makes an authed render publicly cacheable (/account/foo.css)
predicts: Find the unkeyed input or the deceptive-suffix URL that makes a logged-in response cacheable, poison it, then retrieve it COOKIELESSLY. Prove it leaks a username/CSRF token/session — that is the ATO. Scan unkeyed inputs with Param-Miner-style fuzzing, not by hand.

sources.work: Web Cache Deception Attack (Black Hat USA)
Practical Web Cache Poisoning: Redefining "Unexploitable" (PortSwigger Research)

name: Shared cache key not tenant-scoped → cross-tenant data crossing
tells: a performance cache (prompt cache, response cache) keyed on content/prefix
two orgs/keys that can produce the same prefix
a cache_control or ETag the client influences
predicts: Treat the cache key as an authz boundary: send the same cacheable prefix from tenant A and tenant B. If B gets A's cached completion (or a timing/billing oracle shows a shared entry), the key is not org-scoped — a cross-tenant inference/data leak. The move is Kettle's 'what is actually in the cache key', applied to the tenant dimension.

sources.work: Practical Web Cache Poisoning + Web Cache Entanglement (the cache-key-scope question)

name: Token/signed-identifier bound to the wrong audience → cross-service read
tells: an OAuth AS that reflects a client-supplied resource=/audience into the token
a signed/encrypted resource identifier replayed between services
redirect/postMessage leakage of an auth code or token
predicts: Mint or capture a credential issued for audience X and present it to service Y. For OAuth: abuse an 'abnormal' flow (dirty-dancing redirect/postMessage leak) to steal the code, or bind resource= to a second service and confirm Y accepts it. Do NOT forge crypto or test other tenants without authorization — only replay a legitimately-issued identifier.

sources.work: Account hijacking using "dirty dancing" in sign-in OAuth-flows
A New Era of SSRF — parser/audience confusion between a validator and a consumer

name: Prompt injection → tool call → exfil / SSRF sink
tells: an LLM/agent deployment exposed to attacker-controlled text (docs MCP, support bot, RAG)
a tool in reach that reads non-public data or fetches an attacker host
rendered markdown/images that can carry data out
predicts: Enumerate the toolset, then compose: injected instruction → a tool that reads sensitive data or fetches a URL → an exfil sink (image beacon, link, outbound fetch). Re-enumerate the toolset after every version bump — a new tool re-arms the chain. The content boundary, not the model, is the vuln.

sources.work: Embrace The Red — LLM prompt-injection → tool-invocation data exfiltration

name: Hunt the youngest-surface quartile, not the hardened core
tells: a feature shipped in the last weeks (frontier: date)
multi-tenant isolation added AFTER the core was built
GA/beta flags, new /v2 sub-resources
predicts: Rank every surface by ship-date and aim at the newest — isolation bugs live in new features before they are hardened, and the fleet's disproving power is wasted on a fail-closed mature core. (This is why pihunt-authz tags each resource with a frontier: date and ties rank by youth.)

sources.work: The Bug Hunter's Methodology (TBHM) — attack-surface discovery & new-asset prioritization
